name: Swiss Life Holding AG
subsector: Life insurance, pensions and asset management
accounting_notes: Swiss Life adopted IFRS 17 and IFRS 9 on 1 January 2023 (comparatives restated). The starter dataset keeps 2021–2022 on the IFRS 4 basis as originally reported, so there is an accounting break between 2022 and 2023.
capital_regime: Swiss Solvency Test (SST); EU subsidiaries under Solvency II
annual_report_hint: swisslife.com → Investors → Results and reports. The Annual Report contains the segment reporting (Switzerland, France, Germany, International, Asset Managers) and the IFRS consolidated financial statements; the SST ratio is published separately (and in the Financial Condition Report).
data_source: Starter values from a third-party data vendor (FMP via Bigdata.com); sector KPIs are left for you to collect.

what_it_does.reference: Swiss Life is a leading European provider of life insurance, pensions and financial solutions, and one of Europe's largest real-estate asset managers. It insures individuals and companies (including Swiss occupational pensions under the BVG), sells advice through its own financial-advisory networks, and manages assets for third parties (Swiss Life Asset Managers).

key_points.point: Asset management for third parties (incl. real estate)

how_money.reference: Three earnings sources: (1) the savings/investment result — the spread between investment returns and guaranteed or credited rates on policyholder savings; (2) the risk result — premiums for death and disability cover minus claims; (3) the fee result — fees from third-party asset management, advisory networks and unit-linked business. Swiss Life has been shifting towards fee income to reduce capital intensity.

segments.reference: Switzerland, France, Germany, International, Asset Managers.

customers.reference: Private clients (life and pension products), companies and their employees (group life / BVG occupational pensions), high-net-worth clients (International, private placement life insurance) and institutional investors (asset management).

markets.reference: Switzerland (largest), France and Germany, plus Luxembourg, Liechtenstein and Singapore (International).

advantages.reference: Market leader in Swiss group life (BVG); scale in real-estate asset management; owned advisory networks in Germany and France (control of distribution); strong brand and solvency; diversified earnings with a growing fee share.

threats.reference: Interest-rate risk (low rates squeeze the savings spread on guaranteed business); real-estate valuation risk (large real-estate portfolio); regulatory and political risk (BVG reform, the 'legal quote' profit-sharing rules, SST); longevity risk; competition in advisory; market downturns hitting fee income.

events.title: Rising interest rates cut IFRS 4 equity
events.detail: Bond prices fell as rates rose in 2022. Under IFRS 4/IAS 39, unrealised losses on available-for-sale bonds reduced equity through other comprehensive income (OCI) — while the matching decrease in the economic value of liabilities was not fully reflected. Net income was unaffected; equity fell sharply.
events.where_to_verify: Statement of comprehensive income (OCI); statement of changes in equity; notes on financial assets.

events.title: Adoption of IFRS 17 and IFRS 9
events.detail: From 2023 insurance revenue replaces premiums (investment components are excluded), the unearned profit on in-force business sits in the contractual service margin (a liability), and equity is measured differently. Revenue and equity before and after 2023 are not comparable — the decline is accounting-driven, not a collapse in business.
events.where_to_verify: Annual Report 2023: note on changes in accounting policies / transition to IFRS 17 and IFRS 9 (restated 2022 comparatives).

events.title: Share buybacks and rising dividends
events.detail: Swiss Life returned capital through buybacks, reducing the share count, which supports EPS growth beyond net income growth.
events.where_to_verify: Statement of changes in equity (treasury shares); EPS note; capital management section.

top_risks_reference.why: The savings result depends on the spread between investment yields and guaranteed rates; low or falling rates and reinvestment risk compress margins and the SST ratio.
A large real-estate and equity exposure plus fee income linked to asset values: a property downturn hits investment results, solvency and asset-management fees.
Swiss pension politics (BVG conversion rate, legal quote) and SST changes can cap profitability of the Swiss group-life business and change capital requirements.

audit_focus: Measurement of insurance contract liabilities under IFRS 17 (assumptions, contractual service margin)
Valuation of investment property and Level 3 financial assets
Goodwill and intangible assets impairment testing
IT controls over actuarial and investment systems

quiz.prompt: Swiss Life's revenue in the starter data drops from about CHF 20bn (2022) to about CHF 15bn (2023). What is the main reason?
options: Adoption of IFRS 17 changed the revenue definition
Swiss Life lost a third of its clients
quiz.explanation: IFRS 17 insurance revenue excludes investment components (savings deposits). The drop is accounting-driven.

quiz.prompt: Which earnings source has Swiss Life been deliberately growing to reduce capital intensity?
quiz.explanation: Fee income needs little solvency capital compared with guaranteed savings business.
